subject: asteroid ocean impact
title: What If an Asteroid Hit the Ocean Instead of Land?

scenes.text: What if an asteroid hit the ocean? The tsunami isn't the problem. The sky is.
Seventy percent of Earth is water, so most rocks would splash down. Los Alamos scientists simulated a 250-metre asteroid.
The splash climbs tens of kilometres, waves near impact top 400 metres, but they're short and choppy and fade fast.
A real tsunami's waves are over 100 kilometres long. An impact can't make those. Away from the shore, the coast is mostly safe.
The real damage: up to 250 million tonnes of seawater turned to vapour and thrown into the stratosphere.
That vapour lingers for months or years and heats the planet. The ocean doesn't stop an asteroid. It changes the weapon.

description:
What if an asteroid hit the ocean instead of land? Water covers 70 percent of Earth, so most impacts would. Simulations by Galen Gisler's team at Los Alamos National Laboratory, presented in 2016, found a 250-metre asteroid would throw up a splash tens of kilometres high and waves of about 400 metres near the impact, but those waves are short and dispersive and lose energy quickly, unlike real tsunamis whose wavelengths exceed 100 kilometres, so only an impact close to shore is dangerous for coasts. The bigger effect is up to 250 million tonnes of water vaporised and injected into the stratosphere, where it can persist for months to years and affect the climate.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: It has happened: 2.5 million years ago the Eltanin asteroid, 1 to 4 kilometres wide, hit the Pacific near Antarctica. Would you rather it landed on land or at sea?
